title: Indian Psychology — Foundations
summary: Indian psychology rooted in Hinduism, Buddhism and Sufism; orthodox (āstika) and heterodox (nāstika) schools; pramāṇa (means of knowledge); the four Vedas; rasa–bhāva theory; Sāṅkhya versus Advait Vedānta.

notes.t: Indian psychology is the system of psychology rooted in ancient Indian philosophical traditions such as Hinduism, Buddhism and Sufism, focusing on understanding the mind, consciousness and the self. Its core aim is self-realisation and liberation (moksha) by transcending the limitations of ego and material existence.

r: Orthodox (āstika) — accept the authority of the Vedas
Nyāya (logic and reasoning), Vaiśeṣika (atomic theory and metaphysics), Sāṅkhya, Yoga, Mīmāṃsā, Vedānta
Heterodox (nāstika) — do not accept the authority of the Vedas

notes.t: Indian epistemology identifies several valid means (pramāṇa) of gaining knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna). The process of knowing involves four essential factors: pramātā (knower/subject), prameya (object of knowledge), pramāṇa (means of knowledge) and pramā (true knowledge).

r: Direct knowledge through the sense organs.
Knowledge gained from reliable speech or scriptures.
Assumption of an unseen fact to explain something.

notes.t: The Vedas are the oldest sacred texts; the word 'Veda' means knowledge. They were orally passed from one generation to another (śruti, 'heard') and are believed to be of divine origin (apauruṣeya — not created by humans). Structure: the Vedas are divided into four parts — Saṃhitā, Brāhmaṇas, Āraṇyakas and Upanishads (also called Vedānta).

r: Collection of 1,028 hymns in 10 maṇḍalas; oldest Veda; begins with 'Agnimile Purohitam'; 10th Maṇḍala has Puruṣa Sūkta; Gayatri Mantra (3rd Maṇḍala); deities: Indra, Agni, Viṣṇu, Varuṇa, Aditi, Uṣa
Chants and musical hymns; oldest music book; used in ritual chanting; Upanishads: Chāndogya and Kena
Mantras and rituals for yajnas; divided into Śukla (White) and Kṛṣṇa (Black); Upanishads: Bṛhadāraṇyaka, Kaṭha; deals with Yama (god of death)
Spells, charms, healing rituals, daily prayers; 20 khaṇḍas; practical aspects: health, protection; Upanishads: Muṇḍaka, Māṇḍūkya; 'Vasudhaiva Kuṭumbakam' quote

notes.t: The Nāṭyaśāstra is an ancient treatise on the performing arts, attributed to Bharata Muni (c. 200 BCE–200 CE). Bharata introduced the rasa–bhāva theory: rasa is the emotional essence experienced by the audience; bhāva is the emotion or state portrayed by the performer. According to Bharata, rasa arises from bhāva, creating an emotional impact on the audience.

Sāṅkhya philosophy holds that Prakṛti (matter) and Puruṣa (consciousness) are different — a dualist position. Advait Vedānta (monist philosophy) holds that Prakṛti and Puruṣa comprise the same cosmic energy.
Indian psychology's core aim is self-realisation and liberation (moksha). Orthodox (āstika) schools accept Vedic authority; heterodox (nāstika) schools do not. The six pramāṇa are frequently tested.
